title: Dual-core on a single die as the POWER4 organizing principle
where_in_paper: Introduction / overview; 'guiding principles' framing early in the paper
decision: Implement POWER4 as two identical processor cores on a single die, sharing an L2 controller and L3 directory interface, rather than as a single larger monolithic core at the same frequency.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against a single large monolithic core on frequency/area/yield grounds and frames the dual-core SMP-on-a-d approach as the way to scale system throughput within a fixed frequency and power envelope.
rationale: Area, frequency, and yield trade-offs make a single large monolithic core less attractive than two moderate-complexity cores delivering higher aggregate throughput at the same clock.
outcome: The paper reports a 1.3 GHz target frequency a dual-core die that fits within the available frequency/power/yield envelope, positioning POWER4 as an SMP building block.

title: Modest clock-frequency target chosen over highest possible frequency
decision: Target a clock frequency that balanced against complexity, frequency ramp, and design-for-testability, rather than pushing for the absolute highest frequency at the expense of other goals.
alternatives_or_rejected: A more aggressive single-frequency target; the paper explicitly discusses choosing a frequency the design could robustly meet across process and operating conditions.
rationale: Robust frequency across voltage/temperature and across process variation, plus DFM/DFT headroom, was preferred over a headline frequency number.
outcome: 1.3 GHz chosen as the target; the paper frames this as a deliberate trade.

title: Distributed on-chip L2 with a shared L3 controller and directory
decision: Use a distributed on-chip L2 (per-core L2 with shared controller) coordinated with an on-chip L3 controller and directory, rather than a single monolithic L2.
alternatives_or_rejected: A single unified L2 cache was implicitly the alternative being argued against; the paper argues for distributed L2 plus a shared controller/directory for SMP scaling.
rationale: Distributed L2 enables per-core latency/hit-rate characteristics while a shared controller/directory provides coherency and SMP scalability.
outcome: The paper describes the resulting L2/L3 organization and its role in the dual protocol.

title: RAS-first design philosophy-retry and error isolation
decision: Treat-availability-serviceability (RAS) as a first-class design goal, with mechanisms for error detection, isolation, and recovery (hardware retry, fault isolation between cores, redundant structures where needed).
alternatives_or_rejected: A leaner implementation without these RAS hooks; the paper argues these are necessary for the server-class target.
rationale: Server workloads demand continued correct operation in the presence of soft errors; RAS features must be designed in, not bolted on.
outcome: The paper describes specific RAS mechanisms built into the dual-core die, including isolation between cores and recovery paths.

title: Chip-to-chip interconnect organized around a directory-based coherence protocol
decision: Use a directory-based coherence protocol for chip-to-chip SMP scaling rather than a snoop-based protocol, given the shared L3 controller and projected system sizes.
alternatives_or_rejected: Snoop-based coherence; the paper argues against pure snoop at the projected system scale in favor of directory-based coherence with the on-chip L3 directory.
rationale: Snoop traffic scales poorly with system size; directory-based coherence with an on-chip directory scales more cleanly.
outcome: The paper describes the interconnect protocol and how the on-chip directory participates in chip-to-chip coherence.
